explain.say: Staples come in a strip, lightly glued together, held in a channel inside the top arm. When you press the top down, it swings on a hinge at the back.

explain.say: Inside, a thin metal blade called the driver sits right above the front staple. Pressing pushes the blade down, which breaks one staple off the strip and drives it through the paper.

faq.q: Why does the top of a stapler hinge?
faq.a: The hinge at the back lets the top arm swing down like a lever, pushing the driver blade straight onto the front staple.
asks: How does pressing a stapler work?

faq.a: The driver is a thin steel blade the width of one staple. It breaks the front staple off the glued strip and pushes it down through the paper.

faq.q: What is the metal plate under a stapler?
faq.a: It is the anvil. Its curved grooves bend the staple's legs inward under the paper so the staple grips the sheets.
asks: How does a stapler bend the staple?

faq.q: Why does a stapler have a spring inside?
faq.a: A spring in the staple channel pushes the strip forward so the next staple is always under the driver. Another spring lifts the top arm back up.
asks: How does the next staple move forward?

faq.a: If a staple bends sideways or the paper is too thick, the driver can crush it in the channel. Using the right size staples and not overloading the paper helps.

facts: Most office staples come in strips held together by a thin layer of glue.
Rotating the anvil makes the legs bend outward, which is called pinning.
